title: Question 7
stem:
The circuit for an inverting amplifier incorporating an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp) is shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: explain why point $P$ is known as a virtual earth
hints: Hint 1: Start by looking at where the non-inverting (+) input of the op-amp is connected in Fig. 7.1 and what its potential must therefore be.
Hint 2: Recall the golden rule for an ideal op-amp in negative feedback - with its huge open-loop gain, what must be true about the difference between the $V_{+}$ and $V_{-}$ inputs?
Hint 3: Think about why we say virtual rather than real earth - is point P directly wired to earth, and does any current flow into the op-amp input itself?
parts.proper_answer: The non-inverting input is connected to $0\text{ V}$. For an ideal op-amp the open-loop gain is very large so $V_{-} \approx V_{+} \approx 0\text{ V}$. Point P is at earth potential but is not directly connected to earth, and no current enters the op-amp.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the earthed input**
You are sitting with the circuit, so first check the + input. It is wired straight to the $0\text{ V}$ earth line, so $V_{+} = 0\text{ V}$. That is a real earth.

Step 2: **Use the huge gain rule**
An ideal op-amp has an extremely large open-loop gain $A_{0}$. Since $V_{OUT} = A_{0}(V_{+} - V_{-})$ and $V_{OUT}$ must stay finite, the difference $(V_{+} - V_{-})$ must be almost zero. So $$V_{-} \approx V_{+}$$

Step 3: **Why P is at 0 V but only virtually**
Point P is the inverting (-) input, so $V_{P} = V_{-} \approx 0\text{ V}$. It behaves like earth for potentials, but it is not a wire to earth. Also for an ideal op-amp no current flows into the inputs, so all the input current must go through the $5.2\text{ k}\Omega$ feedback resistor. That is why we call it a virtual earth.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: calculate the gain of the amplifier.
hints: Hint 1: Identify this as a classic inverting amplifier and recall which two resistors set the closed-loop gain.
Hint 2: Remember the minus sign for phase inversion and check the values $5.2\text{ k}\Omega$ and $0.80\text{ k}\Omega$ are in the same units before dividing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the inverting gain formula**
For negative feedback with no current into the op-amp, the currents through the input and feedback resistors are equal. This gives the famous result $$G = \frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_{f}}{R_{in}}$$ The minus sign simply means the output is inverted relative to the input.

Step 2: **Put the numbers in**
Here $R_{in} = 0.80\text{ k}\Omega$ and $R_{f} = 5.2\text{ k}\Omega$: $$G = -\frac{5.2\text{ k}\Omega}{0.80\text{ k}\Omega} = -6.5$$ No unit conversion is needed because both are in $\text{k}\Omega$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
When the op-amp is saturated, the potential difference across the LED is $2.3\text{ V}$.

Calculate the minimum resistance of resistor $R$ so that the current in the LED is limited to $30\text{ mA}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what $V_{OUT}$ must be when this op-amp saturates positively, given its $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$ supplies and the direction the LED needs to conduct.
Hint 2: Look at the series loop of R and the LED connected between $V_{OUT}$ and earth, and use Kirchhoff to find how much of $V_{OUT}$ is left across R if the LED drops $2.3\text{ V}$.
Hint 3: You now know the p.d. across R and the maximum allowed current of $30\text{ mA}$ - consider which law links $V$, $I$ and $R$ to find the minimum $R$.
parts.proper_answer: At saturation $V_{OUT} = +5.0\text{ V}$. p.d. across R $= 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ V}$. With $I = 30\text{ mA}$, $R = 2.7 / 0.030 = 90\, \Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the saturated output**
The op-amp is powered between $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$, so it saturates at about the supply rails. To light the LED with conventional current flowing down through R and D to earth, $V_{OUT}$ must be positive, so $$V_{OUT} = +5.0\text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Apply Kirchhoff to the output loop**
R and the LED are in series between $V_{OUT}$ and $0\text{ V}$. The voltages must add to $V_{OUT}$: $$V_{R} + V_{LED} = V_{OUT}$$ With $V_{LED} = 2.3\text{ V}$: $$V_{R} = 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ V}$$

Step 3: **Use Ohm's law to limit the current**
The same current flows in R and the LED. For the limiting case $I = 30\text{ mA} = 0.030\text{ A}$: $$R = \frac{V_{R}}{I} = \frac{2.7}{0.030} = 90\, \Omega$$ A smaller R would let more than $30\text{ mA}$ flow, so $90\, \Omega$ is the minimum safe value.
